paragraphs.source_en:
(1826) gives a presumably imaginary account of the accidental discovery by Mary and her ‘companion’
of the cave of the Cumaean sybil, during a visit to Naples in 1818: ‘At length my friend, who had taken
up some of the leaves strewed about, exclaimed, “This is the Sibyl’s cave; these are Sibylline leaves.”
 On examination, we found that all the leaves, bark, and other substances, were traced with written
characters. What appeared to us more astonishing, was that these writings were expressed in various
languages: some unknown to my companion, ancient Chaldee, and Egyptian hieroglyphics, old as the
Pyramids. Stranger still, some were in modern dialects, English and Italian. We could make out little
by the dim light, but they seemed to contain prophecies, detailed relations of events but lately passed;
names, now well known, but of modern date; and often exclamations of exultation or woe, of victory
